Empirical Research Plan  
“State Corporate-Tax Changes and Firm Leverage, 1990–2011”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented with an event-study.  
• Why DID?  State corporate tax schedules change at different calendar years and by different magnitudes.  Firms are “as-good-as-randomly” exposed to these shocks depending on the state in which they are chartered / headquartered (Compustat’s state of incorporation or HQ).  This creates a panel with plausibly exogenous within-state, within-firm variation.  
• Why not IV or RDD?  We do not observe a sharp cutoff that forces some firms to be taxed differently, and suitable external instruments for state tax rates are scarce.  DID directly exploits the policy variation and facilitates event-time dynamics.

Estimator: Recent literature shows that two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) can be biased with staggered adoption.  I will therefore use (i) Sun & Abraham (2020) interaction-weighted event-study and (ii) Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) group-time ATT estimators, both implemented in R (fixest + did or did2s packages).  A continuous tax-rate DID will also be run:

Leverage_{ist} = β · TaxRate_{st} + X_{it}′γ + η_s + λ_t + ε_{ist}

where β is interpreted as the semi-elasticity of leverage with respect to the statutory rate.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
• Treatment variable  
  – Preferred spec: continuous statutory state corporate tax rate τ_{st}.  
  – Binary alternative: indicator Treat_{st}=1 in years t ≥ year of first ≥1 pp increase (or decrease) for a given state.  We run separate “tax-increase” and “tax-cut” samples.  

• Control group / counterfactual  
  – Firms in states that did not change their tax rate in that calendar year (and, in the binary design, have yet to be treated).  Dynamic methods ensure only not-yet-treated groups serve as controls.  

• Treatment timing  
  – Event date g_s = first year in which state s implements the focal tax change.  
  – Event time k = t – g_s (k=0 is the first year of the new rate).  Leads k<0 test pre-trends; lags k>0 capture persistence.  

• Running variable, cutoff: not applicable (not RDD).

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends (counterfactual leverage in treated and control states would have evolved similarly absent the tax change).  
  Plausibility: States do not coordinate tax changes with trends in firms’ capital structure. We can bolster by controlling for state-specific linear or industry×state trends and by visual pre-trend tests.

A2. No differential anticipation.  Firms do not significantly change leverage in advance of a just-announced tax bill.  
  Plausibility: State tax legislation is often negotiated within the fiscal year; corporate financing decisions have lags.  We check by estimating leads; insignificant coefficients support plausibility.

A3. Stable unit treatment value / no spillovers across states.  
  Plausibility: Some multi-state firms can shift debt; we use headquarters state, but will later restrict to single-state firms and add multi-state controls.

A4. Exogeneity of timing / magnitude of tax changes with respect to firm-level shocks.  
  Plausibility: State fiscal stress could correlate with local economic downturns that influence leverage (downward bias).  We address by controlling for state-year macro covariates and employing an IV robustness (lagged partisan composition predicting tax changes).

-------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations  

Threat 1: Policy endogeneity to state business cycles.  
• Mitigation: Add state-year unemployment rate, GSP growth; include state-specific linear and quadratic trends; implement placebo tests on non-tax states.

Threat 2: Heterogeneous treatment effects & TWFE bias.  
• Mitigation: Use interaction-weighted estimators (Sun–Abraham) and group-time ATT (Callaway–Sant’Anna) rather than vanilla TWFE. Compare results.

Threat 3: Cross-border / multi-state income shifting.  
• Mitigation: (i) Limit to firms incorporated and operating >90 % of sales in one state for baseline; (ii) weight by in-state sales apportionment where available; (iii) show robustness to excluding Fortune-100 firms with extensive subsidiaries.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)           # fast TWFE + SA event study
library(did)              # Callaway–Sant'Anna
library(ggplot2)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
comp <- fread("compustat_firmyear_1990_2011.csv")   # contains gvkey, year, state, financials
tax  <- fread("state_corp_tax_1990_2011.csv")        # state, year, stat_tax_rate

# merge
dat <- merge(comp, tax, by = c("state","year"))

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
dat[, leverage := total_debt / total_assets]
dat[, lsize    := log(total_assets)]
dat[, profitability := ebitda / total_assets]

# create continuous treatment
dat[, treat_cont := stat_tax_rate]      # percentage points, e.g. 6.5 -> 0.065

# Binary treatment for first ≥1pp tax increase
setorder(dat, state, year)
dat[, d_tax := stat_tax_rate - shift(stat_tax_rate, 1L, type="lag"), by = state]
dat[, first_inc_year := ifelse(d_tax >= 0.01 & !duplicated(state[d_tax >= 0.01]), year, NA), by=state]
dat[, g := min(first_inc_year, na.rm=TRUE), by=state]
dat[g == Inf, g := NA]                  # never treated states

dat[, treat_bin := as.integer(!is.na(g) & year >= g)]

# Event time for Sun–Abraham
dat[, event_time := year - g]           # NA for never treated

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main Regression — Continuous TWFE
spec1 <- feols(leverage ~ treat_cont + lsize + profitability | state + year, data = dat, cluster = ~state)
summary(spec1)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. Sun & Abraham Event-study (fixest 0.10+)
spec_sa <- feols(leverage ~ sunab(g, year) + lsize + profitability |
                 state + year, data = dat, cluster = ~state)
iplot(spec_sa)     # graph leads/lags

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5. Callaway–Sant'Anna ATT(g,t)
cs_data <- dat[!is.na(g)]               # keep groups with adoption
att_gt  <- att_gt(yname   = "leverage",
                  gname   = "g",
                  tname   = "year",
                  idname  = "gvkey",
                  xformla = ~ lsize + profitability,
                  data    = cs_data)
summary(att_gt)
ggdid(att_gt)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness Check: single-state firms only
single_state <- dat[num_states_operated==1]  # assume variable exists
spec_rob <- feols(leverage ~ treat_cont + lsize + profitability | state + year,
                  data = single_state, cluster = ~state)
etable(spec1, spec_rob)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  

Theory: The marginal benefit of debt equals τ·r (interest tax shield).  An increase in the statutory rate raises this benefit, so we expect a positive semi-elasticity.  However, most variation is in statutory state rate (often 0–12 %), whereas the federal rate is ~35 % over the sample; hence the total tax shield marginally increases.  Prior evidence (e.g., Graham 2000) suggests a 1 pp increase in combined tax rate raises target debt/asset ratio by roughly 0.5–1.0 pp.  Because state rates are only a share of the total, I expect:

β ≈ +0.06 to +0.10 (i.e., a 1 pp ↑ in state rate → 6–10 bps ↑ in leverage ratio)  
Sign: positive.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  

C1: Parallel pre-trends evidenced by insignificant leads        … 1  
C2: No anticipation / timing exogenous                           … 0.5  
C3: No spillovers / SUTVA                                         … 0.5  
C4: Correct estimator for staggered adoption (SA / CS)           … 1  
C5: Robustness to alternative samples & controls                 … 1  

Total = 4 / 5 (overall credible).
